tldr: This is a loose cluster of mostly arXiv papers, not one developing story. It began as broad agent training, retrieval and alignment work, then re-centered in November on RL itself: agent and multi-agent RL, RL-learned memory, training cost, and tool-use reliability.
whats_new: Nov 19: two continual-RL papers (policy-improvement-guided replay, grid-cell successor features) target learning new tasks without losing old ones, after StateAlign showed RL tool-use gains can raise tool hallucination.
why_it_matters: If you post-train or operate tool-using agents, this cluster names concrete costs of RL: rollout underutilization, tool hallucination that rises with task score, and crude stop rules, but nearly every result is author-reported.

beats.headline: RL methods aim at multi-turn, multi-agent and tool-using agents
beats.summary: Open multi-agent foundations, JHiMA-WebRL, targeted guidance, Octopus latent-KV sub-agents, and a study of what multi-turn RL actually improves.

beats.headline: RL is used to learn what to keep: prompt compression, incremental summaries and world-model memory
beats.summary: EffComp, the Twists and Turns long-term memory benchmark, MaxIM, and test-time model-based RL for memory.

beats.headline: RL training cost gets attacked from sampler, scheduler and serving stack
beats.summary: FewStepRL, the ASP rollout scheduler, LM-SimBench for parallelism choices, and vLLM's TPU v7 co-design reporting a 107x cycle speedup.

beats.headline: Better task scores can mean more tool hallucination, so papers add state-awareness, scaffolds and stop rules
beats.summary: AutoScaffold, StateAlign, Learn then Bet intervention rules, AutoRL, imitation-bootstrapped MARL, and safe in-context RL under a cost budget.

beats.headline: Applied RL papers and an unrelated hallucination benchmark ride along on shared vocabulary
beats.summary: Interactive HTML generation, ReShap interpretability, RLDE document editing, and a Bengali hallucination benchmark.

beats.headline: Continual RL: learning new tasks without losing old ones
beats.summary: Policy-improvement-guided replay and grid cells as spectral successor features.

open_questions: Does StateAlign's reduction in tool hallucination hold on tool APIs outside the paper's own benchmarks?
Does vLLM's 107x RL cycle speedup on TPU v7 carry over to policies larger than Qwen3-0.6B?
Do learned intervention rules like Learn then Bet beat turn limits on production agent runs without stopping good runs early?
Does RL-learned memory (MaxIM, EffComp) beat plain summarization or truncation once training cost is counted?
Do the continual-RL methods keep old skills when applied to LLM post-training rather than control tasks?
take_for_builders: Before adopting an RL-tuned tool-use model, track tool-hallucination rate (calls to tools that do not fit the state) alongside task success in your evals, since the two can move in opposite directions.
